parole.significato: shoo (call usually directed at a creature to drive it away)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Turkic. Compare Russian кыш (kyš), German ksch.

parole.significato: lasso, lazo (long rope with a sliding loop on one end, generally used in ranching to catch cattle and horses)

parole.testo: Probably a post-Mongol invasion Turkic borrowing via Ukrainian бу́рий (búryj). Compare Russian бу́рый (búryj).

parole.significato: type of noblemen's clothing of eastern origin worn in Poland in the eighteenth century
parole.testo: Derived from Turkic, compare Russian чекме́нь (čekménʹ), Tatar чикмән (çikmän), dialectal Turkish çekmen. First attested in 1760. Compare also sukmana and kopieniak.

parole.significato: one-sided and colorful oriental carpet for floor covering or wall hanging
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Turkic. Compare Czech koberec and Russian ковёр (kovjór).
Borrowed from Turkic, from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid). Compare Kazakh мешіт (mešit), Tatar мәчет (mäçet), Turkish mescit, Turkmen metjit.
Borrowed from a Turkic language. Compare Bashkir айғыр (ayğır), Kashubian jedżer, Old Turkic 𐰑𐰍𐰺 (adɣïr), Serbo-Croatian ajgir /ајгир, and Ukrainian о́гир (óhyr). Displaced Old Polish świerzepic.

parole.significato: horse archer's archery equipment consisting of a bow with its bow case and arrows in a quiver
parole.testo: From a Turkic language. Compare Ukrainian сагайда́к (sahajdák).

parole.significato: horse archer's archery equipment consisting of a bow with its bow case and arrows in a quiver
sukmana (type of traditional coat once worn by peasants in Poland)
parole.testo: Derived from Turkic, contaminated with sukno (“cloth”), as also happened in Bulgarian сукма́н (sukmán). Compare czekman and kopieniak.

parole.significato: Tatar (a member of one of several Turkic ethnic groups)
parole.testo: Derived from Turkic. Doublet of Tatarzyn.

parole.significato: Tatar (member of one of several Turkic ethnic groups)
parole.testo: Derived from Turkic. Doublet of Tatar. Displaced by Tatar, except in the proverb złapał Kozak Tatarzyna, a Tatarzyn za łeb trzyma.
